question: An HR partner suspects that Claude's candidate summaries describe some applicants more warmly than others for reasons unrelated to their experience. Which sequence of steps is correct?
options: A) Compare the wording across the results; agree what an even summary should contain; run closely comparable profiles; decide whether the difference is systematic.
B) Run closely comparable profiles; agree what an even summary should contain; decide whether the difference is systematic; compare the wording across the results.
C) Agree what an even summary should contain; compare the wording across the results; decide whether the difference is systematic; run closely comparable profiles.
D) Agree what an even summary should contain; run closely comparable profiles; compare the wording across the results; decide whether the difference is systematic.
correct_answers: D) Agree what an even summary should contain; run closely comparable profiles; compare the wording across the results; decide whether the difference is systematic.
explanations: Incorrect. There is nothing to compare until the comparable profiles have been run, so this ordering puts the comparison before the material it needs.
Incorrect. Deciding whether a difference is systematic before the wording has been compared reverses the two steps that carry the evidence.
Incorrect. The comparable profiles are the test itself, so running them last means the conclusion was reached without them.
Correct. A standard has to exist before wording can be judged against it, comparable profiles create a fair test, and only then does a difference in wording mean anything.
